---
title: "Resources"
subtitle: "Sources used so far, annotated"
---

Every source listed here is used to *ground* claims in the course (each
also appears in `sources/source-map.md` and `sources/claims.csv` with
exact locators) and is annotated as a *learning* resource in its own
right, in case you want to go to the original. The first three anchor the
softmax, neural-network, and why-transformers lessons; the rest were added
for the later sections of `learn/why-transformers.qmd` and for the two
text-to-numbers lessons.

The full course will eventually distinguish a bounded set of evidentiary
sources from a larger, curated resource library organized into learning
paths. This page is the seed of that library — only what has actually been
used so far, not a preview of the eventual full list.

---

### 3Blue1Brown, *Transformers, the tech behind LLMs*

- **Creator:** Grant Sanderson (3Blue1Brown)
- **Format:** video, ~27 minutes total; the relevant segment starts at
  22:22 ("Softmax with temperature") and runs about 4 minutes
- **Level:** introductory, strongly visual
- **What it explains particularly well:** why softmax needs the
  normalizing sum, and how temperature reshapes the distribution — with a
  direct animated derivation that this course's static equations cannot
  fully replicate
- **Recommended start:** 22:22
- **Why included:** the clearest available visual counterpart to the
  softmax equation and temperature behavior taught in
  `learn/softmax-sampling.qmd`
- **Limitation:** does not discuss the multinomial-logit connection, or
  where that analogy breaks down — that framing is this course's own
  contribution, not the video's
- **Link:** <https://www.3blue1brown.com/lessons/gpt>

### Andrej Karpathy, *Deep Dive into LLMs like ChatGPT*

- **Creator:** Andrej Karpathy
- **Format:** video, 3 hours 31 minutes total; the relevant segment
  ("inference") starts at 26:01 and runs about 5 minutes
- **Level:** introductory, plain-language, no equations
- **What it explains particularly well:** what sampling looks like inside
  a real autoregressive generation loop — one token drawn, appended, and
  fed back in — which grounds why "the same prompt can produce different
  answers" in an actual running system, not just in the abstract
- **Recommended start:** 26:01
- **Why included:** the principal narrative anchor for this whole course;
  this segment specifically supports the sampling and inference claims
  used in this slice
- **Limitation:** purely conceptual — no equations, and the segment alone
  does not cover pretraining, post-training, or tokenization, all of which
  are addressed elsewhere in the video and in later modules not yet built
- **Link:** <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7xTGNNLPyMI&t=1561s>

### Vaswani et al., *Attention Is All You Need*

- **Creator:** Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit,
  Llion Jones, Aidan N. Gomez, Łukasz Kaiser, Illia Polosukhin (Google
  Brain / Google Research / University of Toronto)
- **Format:** paper, arXiv:1706.03762 (v7, 2023-08-02); Sections 1 and 4
  (a few pages) are the relevant sections for this course so far
- **Level:** technical
- **What it explains particularly well:** the precise, tabulated
  computational trade-offs (complexity per layer, sequential operations,
  maximum path length) between recurrent, convolutional, and self-attention
  layers — Table 1 is the original source for every such figure used in
  `learn/why-transformers.qmd`
- **Recommended start:** Section 1 (Introduction) for the motivation;
  Section 4 ("Why Self-Attention") and its Table 1 for the numbers
- **Why included:** the primary source for the architectural claims in
  `learn/why-transformers.qmd`; verified directly against the live paper
  before any claim citing it was written
- **Limitation:** written for a machine-translation encoder-decoder
  setting, not a modern decoder-only language model, and the paper's tables
  and figures are reproduced here only as short, attributed textual
  descriptions, not copied images — the paper's own license
  (arXiv's non-exclusive distribution license, not a Creative Commons
  license) does not permit unrestricted figure reuse
- **Link:** <https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762>

### Devlin et al., *BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding*

- **Format:** paper, arXiv:1810.04805 (v2, 2019-05-24); the abstract is
  enough for how this course uses it
- **Level:** technical
- **What it explains particularly well:** that one pretrained transformer
  can be adapted to many downstream tasks with minimal task-specific
  architecture, the pretraining-and-transfer step in
  `learn/why-transformers.qmd`
- **Limitation:** an encoder model, not an autoregressive language model
- **Link:** <https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805>

### Kaplan et al., *Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models*

- **Format:** paper, arXiv:2001.08361 (v1, 2020-01-23); the abstract
  states the result used
- **Level:** technical
- **What it explains particularly well:** the empirical regularity that
  language-model loss improves systematically with model size, data, and
  compute over a wide range
- **Limitation:** an empirical regularity for the studied setup, not a law
- **Link:** <https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361>

### Brown et al., *Language Models are Few-Shot Learners*

- **Format:** paper, arXiv:2005.14165 (v4, 2020-07-22); the abstract
  states the results used
- **Level:** technical
- **What it explains particularly well:** that a large autoregressive
  transformer can perform tasks from demonstrations placed in its input,
  without any parameter updates
- **Limitation:** reports observed performance; does not explain the
  mechanism
- **Link:** <https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165>

### Sennrich, Haddow, and Birch, *Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units*

- **Format:** paper, arXiv:1508.07909 (v5, 2016-06-10); the abstract and
  the BPE section are short
- **Level:** technical
- **What it explains particularly well:** why a fixed word vocabulary
  fails on rare and unknown words, and how repeatedly merging frequent
  character pairs produces a subword vocabulary; the basis for
  `learn/tokens-context.qmd` §2–§3
- **Limitation:** written for machine translation, before byte-level
  variants and the space and punctuation rules later tokenizers adopted
- **Link:** <https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.07909>

### Radford et al., *Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners* (GPT-2)

- **Format:** paper (OpenAI, 2019); Section 2.2, "Input Representation",
  is one page
- **Level:** technical
- **What it explains particularly well:** the concrete reasoning behind
  byte-level BPE and the rule that spaces may merge with a following word
  while punctuation may not, in the authors' own words; also the source of
  the 50,257-token vocabulary and 1,024-token context figures used in the
  text-to-numbers lessons
- **Limitation:** describes one 2019 tokenizer; current tokenizers differ
  in details
- **Link:** <https://cdn.openai.com/better-language-models/language_models_are_unsupervised_multitask_learners.pdf>

### Bengio, Ducharme, Vincent, and Jauvin, *A Neural Probabilistic Language Model*

- **Format:** paper, Journal of Machine Learning Research 3 (2003),
  1137–1155; Sections 1 and 2 carry the ideas used
- **Level:** technical
- **What it explains particularly well:** the idea of learning a vector
  for each word jointly with the model that predicts the next word, and
  why similar words end up with similar vectors; the basis for the
  embedding sections of `learn/how-created.qmd` and
  `learn/tokens-context.qmd`
- **Limitation:** the network is not a transformer, and the vocabulary is
  words, not subword tokens
- **Link:** <https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume3/bengio03a/bengio03a.pdf>

### Liu et al., *Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts*

- **Format:** paper, arXiv:2307.03172 (v3, 2023-11-20); the abstract and
  figures carry the main result
- **Level:** technical
- **What it explains particularly well:** empirical evidence that where a
  relevant passage sits in a long input affects how well a model uses it
- **Limitation:** 2023 models; the size of the effect varies by model and
  task
- **Link:** <https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172>

### Lewis et al., *Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks*

- **Format:** paper, arXiv:2005.11401 (v4, 2021-04-12); the abstract is
  enough for how this course uses it
- **Level:** technical
- **What it explains particularly well:** the idea of combining a model's
  fixed parametric knowledge with text retrieved at request time
- **Limitation:** the specific architecture described is one of many ways
  to do retrieval; the course uses only the general idea
- **Link:** <https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401>

### Anthropic, *Context windows* (Claude API documentation)

- **Format:** documentation page, accessed 2026-09-15
- **Level:** practitioner
- **What it explains particularly well:** exactly what counts toward one
  provider's context window and how turns accumulate; the product-specific
  illustration in `learn/tokens-context.qmd` §8–§9
- **Limitation:** product-specific and revised over time; figures are as
  of the access date
- **Link:** <https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows>

### Anthropic, *Effective context engineering for AI agents*

- **Format:** engineering blog post, published 2025-09-29, accessed
  2026-09-15
- **Level:** practitioner
- **What it explains particularly well:** the working definition of
  context as the tokens included when sampling, and the case for treating
  it as a finite resource
- **Limitation:** one provider's guidance about its own models, not a
  peer-reviewed result; this course pairs it with Liu et al. above
- **Link:** <https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents>
